items.question: Explain the prototype chain in JavaScript.
items.answer: Every object has [[Prototype]] accessed via Object.getPrototypeOf. Property reads check own properties first, then walk the chain until null. Constructor functions have a .prototype object; instances from new get that as [[Prototype]]. class extends sets the subclass prototype's [[Prototype]] to the superclass prototype. Method calls are property lookups — not C# virtual tables.
followUps: What happens if you replace Constructor.prototype after creating instances?
items.sixtySeconds: Lookup walks own props then [[Prototype]] chain. new links instance to Constructor.prototype. class is sugar over the same mechanism. instanceof checks prototype linkage.

items.question: Is JavaScript class syntax different from prototypes?
items.answer: No new object model — class desugars to a constructor function and prototype object. extends uses Object.setPrototypeOf on prototypes and copies static inheritance. Methods live on ClassName.prototype. typeof MyClass is function. Derived constructors must call super() before using this. Class field arrows create per-instance functions with lexical this.
followUps: Can a constructor return a different object?
items.sixtySeconds: class is sugar. Prototypes underneath. super before this in derived ctor. Static methods on the function object.

items.question: Walk through the this binding rules.
items.answer: this is set at call time: default binding (strict undefined), implicit (obj.method), explicit (call/apply/bind), new binding (fresh object), arrow lexical (enclosing this). Priority: new beats bind beats implicit beats default; arrows ignore call site. Detaching obj.method loses implicit binding — common in event handlers and setTimeout.
followUps: Predict this inside setTimeout callback in a method.
How do class field arrows fix lost this?
items.sixtySeconds: Five rules at call site. Arrows capture lexical this. const f = obj.m; f() loses implicit binding. Fix with bind, arrow field, or wrapper.

items.question: How do JavaScript private fields differ from TypeScript private and C# private?
items.answer: JavaScript #fields are runtime slots accessible only inside the class lexical body — TypeError outside. TypeScript private is compile-time only and erases to a public property in emitted JS unless you use #. C# private is enforced by CLR metadata at runtime with full access modifier model (protected, internal). Underscore prefix is convention only.
followUps: Can a subclass access a parent # field?
items.sixtySeconds: Three privates: # runtime, TS compile-only, C# CLR. Symbols obscure keys but are not secret.

items.question: Inheritance versus composition in JavaScript?
items.answer: Default to composition: pass store, clock, and clients into factories or constructors. Use extends for small polymorphic surfaces where callers invoke methods on a shared prototype (parse, handle). Mixins copy onto prototypes — watch name collisions. Deep BaseWorker hierarchies are as fragile as in C#. Avoid mutating shared .prototype in libraries.
followUps: What breaks when base constructor calls an overridable method?
items.sixtySeconds: Compose deps for services. extends for shallow is-a polymorphism. Mixins are compromise. Same BaseService smell as C#.

items.question: What are property descriptors and why do they matter?
items.answer: Each property has writable, enumerable, and configurable flags. Literals default all true. Object.defineProperty can lock down assignment or hide keys from Object.keys and JSON.stringify. for...in walks enumerable prototype chain keys — use Object.hasOwn for own keys. Object.freeze is shallow.
followUps: Why might a library set enumerable: false?
items.sixtySeconds: Descriptors control write, enumerate, reconfigure. freeze is shallow. hasOwn filters prototype pollution in loops.

items.question: How is JavaScript OOP different from C# and TypeScript?
items.answer: JavaScript runtime has objects and prototype lookup — no nominal types, no interfaces at runtime, no value types, reference equality with ===. TypeScript adds structural compile-time checks that erase. C# preserves CLR metadata: nominal typing, is/as on interfaces, virtual/override vtables, Equals/GetHashCode, and runtime private. instanceof works for JS classes; TS interfaces throw ReferenceError if used with instanceof.
followUps: Give structural typing example TS allows that C# rejects.
Is JavaScript method dispatch like C# virtual?
items.sixtySeconds: JS: objects + prototypes. TS: erased structural types. C#: CLR metadata. That one split explains privacy, interfaces, equality, and dispatch.

items.question: What is the difference between prototype dispatch and C# virtual dispatch?
items.answer: C# virtual/override fills fixed slots in a method table loaded from metadata — calling through a base reference dispatches to the derived override. JavaScript finds methods by walking the prototype chain; you can mutate Constructor.prototype at runtime and affect instances without own shadow properties. There is no sealed vtable — flexibility with different invariants.
items.sixtySeconds: C# vtable fixed in metadata. JS prototype lookup mutable. class does not add virtual tables.
